analysis.one_liner: Cancels the 2025 across-the-board tariffs and requires Congress to approve future ones.
analysis.headline: The bill to cancel the 2025 tariffs and require congressional approval for new ones has sat without action in committee since its April 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would immediately wipe out three executive orders imposing tariffs — a 10% tariff on most imports, plus 25% tariffs on most goods from Canada and Mexico. Going forward, it would bar the president from imposing or raising tariffs unless both chambers of Congress pass a law approving them. Routine trade remedies like antidumping duties would be left alone.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay higher prices because tariffs are passed through to import costs, import-dependent businesses such as retailers and manufacturers that buy foreign parts, and U.S. exporters hurt by other countries' retaliatory tariffs. Congress would also regain the power to set trade policy that recent presidents have exercised alone.

how_it_helps.text: The bill terminates the duties under Executive Order 14257 (a 10% tariff on most imports plus higher rates on specified partners), Executive Order 14193 (25% on most Canadian imports), and Executive Order 14194 (25% on most Mexican imports), and any substantially similar orders.

It would require an enacted joint resolution of Congress before the president could impose or increase any duty, quota, or tariff-rate quota, restoring congressional control over a power recent presidents have used unilaterally.

It preserves standard trade remedies — antidumping and countervailing duties under the Tariff Act of 1930 and certain other long-standing authorities — so industries facing genuinely unfair imports keep their existing protections.

analysis.who_pays: The president would lose the power to set tariffs by executive order, and federal revenue from the canceled tariffs would end. Domestic industries sheltered by the tariffs — and U.S. negotiators, who would lose tariff threats as bargaining leverage — would bear the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: The president's trade powers and protected industries

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the tariffs removes the protection they were intended to give some U.S. producers and the negotiating leverage tariff threats provide, and the CRS summary notes tariffs were imposed on trading partners as policy pressure.
Tariff collections would end, so the bill would eliminate that federal revenue; tariffs are effectively a tax collected at the border, paid by importers and ultimately passed to consumers.
Requiring a new law for every tariff action could make trade responses slow, since Congress would need to pass a joint resolution each time the executive branch wanted to act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Tariffs on imports function as a tax that lands on U.S. businesses and shoppers, so canceling them puts money back in ordinary households' budgets; that is the core benefit. The honest cost is that the tariffs may have been doing something for some protected industries and for negotiating leverage, and Congress moving slowly could be a real weakness. On balance the bill trades a broad consumer cost for narrower, targeted risks.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees in April 2025, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on April 10, 2025, joined by 20 original cosponsors including members of the Ways and Means Committee's trade subcommittee.

It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and additionally to the Committee on Rules, the standard first step that routes a bill to the panels with jurisdiction over tariffs and floor procedure.
Forty House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors as of the latest count, with no Republicans listed.
After referral, no committee markup, hearing, or floor action has been recorded — the action history ends at the referral.
The tariffs the bill targets remain in effect because the bill has not become law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The president keeps unilateral tariff power, and consumers and importers keep paying the tariffs. Businesses protected by the tariffs also keep their shelter.

for.name: Rep. Linda T. Sánchez

against.name: Ways and Means Committee

against.what_they_did: Has not held a markup or taken any recorded action on the bill since it was referred in April 2025.

against.name: President Trump
against.what_they_did: Imposed the tariffs the bill would terminate through executive orders and has relied on emergency authorities to set trade policy.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republicans have signed on, and the bill sits in committees chaired by the majority party.

industries.industry: Importers, retailers, and manufacturers that buy foreign goods and parts
industries.note: Canceling the tariffs lowers the import costs these businesses pay, which they typically pass on to consumers as prices. Ordinary shoppers and these businesses win together.

industries.industry: Industries protected by the tariffs, such as domestic manufacturers facing import competition
industries.note: Ending the tariffs removes the price cushion the executive orders gave these industries against foreign competition. Their gain under the status quo comes at consumers' expense through higher prices.
The 25% tariffs on most Canadian and Mexican imports would disappear, restoring their access to U.S. buyers and cutting costs for U.S. importers of energy, autos, and food.
The bill strips the president's ability to impose tariffs unilaterally, requiring a joint resolution of Congress for each new duty or quota.

analysis.trajectory: With all-Democratic sponsorship and no committee movement in months, this bill is on the standard path of a minority-party policy bill: it will likely sit in Ways and Means without a markup and expire at the end of the 119th Congress. Similar tariff-termination proposals face the same arithmetic — the majority party's leadership has shown no interest in curtailing the president's tariff authority, so the realistic path to a floor vote is essentially none this Congress.
